answer.rationale: The revised manuscript is essentially the earlier text with added limitation wording and citations; the core design and analysis problems remain. The central claim is that type 3 (image with people) posts generate the most engagement. That claim rests on only 30 posts, a type confounded with topic and content, a pooled engagement metric that is not comparable across platforms, and an under-reported model. The authors' reply to R1 declines to change anything. The reply to R2 says the Discussion was rewritten, but the visible changes are mostly a limitation sentence, a few citations and a future-research line. The speculative interpretation of comments and shares is unchanged. The observable pattern in the figures is consistent with type 3 doing better, but the strength of the causal and practical conclusions exceeds what the design supports.

issues.issue: Causal attribution of engagement to post type is weak. Types were cycled over weeks, so type is confounded with topic and date. Table 2 shows unequal topic distribution across types (e.g., impact noise: 1 type 1 vs 4 type 3). Type 3 also differs from type 2 in several features at once (people, equipment, caption). The four additional type 3 reposts of earlier content are described only briefly, with no numbers, tests or statement of whether the same audience had already seen the content. They are also likely affected by repetition.
issues.response_claim: The authors state the additional type 3 posts were meant to show that differences are due to type, not content. The R2 reply does not address design confounding.
issues.observed_change: No change to the design or the reposting description. Results and Methods text on the four extra posts is unchanged between versions.

evidence.exact_quote: We aimed to verify that the studied differences in engagement can be attributed to different types and not the content.
we discovered that if we share the same content in as different type, the result is the same

issues.issue: Statistical analysis is underspecified and possibly inappropriate. The Poisson mixed model has no reported coefficients, tests, post-type × platform interactions, an overdispersion check, or random-effects structure details. The text says only that unique post ID was a random effect. Phase differences are described only as 'not significant', and a non-significant result is then taken as evidence of no effect for RQ3 and RQ4. The platform comparisons rest on 30 posts and are partly driven by follower count differences, with no exposure offset. The engagement-model results appear only in Figure 9, with a wide LinkedIn interval.
issues.response_claim: None. The authors do not address the statistical reporting; the R1 reviewer rated the analysis appropriate.
issues.observed_change: No added statistics. The only text change is the limitations paragraph.

evidence.exact_quote: The difference between the two phases is not statistically significant when comparing number of likes, impressions and engagement.
time dimension (season) and alternative text does not influence the engagement

evidence.observation: Figure 6 and the engagement figure show wide LinkedIn intervals; no coefficient or test table is given.

issues.issue: The outcome measure is not equivalent across platforms. The pooled 'engagement' is interactions on Twitter and LinkedIn but clicks on Facebook, and 'impressions' pools impressions with Facebook reach. Treating these as 'measuring the same thing' is asserted, not shown. This undermines the cross-platform comparison and the claim that Facebook engagement was lowest. Also, monitoring took place 2 days after posting, while the lifespan figures the authors cite for LinkedIn are longer.
issues.response_claim: The authors say they 'clarified in advance what each parameter means' and that, according to definitions, the metrics measure the same thing.
issues.observed_change: No change; the limitation about comparability adds only a citation to Kietzmann et al.

evidence.exact_quote: according to the definitions they measure the same thing
Comparability of the three social media channels is an additional limitation (Kietzmann et al., 2011).

issues.issue: Interpretation of low comments and shares is speculative. There was 1 comment and 5 shares in total. The claim that users are uncomfortable commenting on sustainable construction topics has no supporting evidence in the study. R2 flagged this directly. The authors reply that it is an 'interoperation' consistent with prior studies and leave the claim unchanged. Related explanations (algorithms, 'war or Brexit' news days) are likewise untested.
issues.response_claim: The authors say the interpretation 'is also in line with previous studies' (Ellison et al., 2014).
issues.observed_change: The claim remains verbatim in the revised text. The Discussion added only limitation text.

evidence.exact_quote: These findings indicate that users may not be comfortable commenting on topics connected to sustainable construction
this is the interoperation of the result which is also in line with previous studies

issues.issue: Conclusions and generalisation are overstated. A single institutional account with about 2,000 followers, one English-language project, one year and an audience that is largely researchers are used to claim that type 3 'is the most effective way to engage social media audiences' and to advise policy makers. The authors added the limitations sentence about generalisability. They did not soften the abstract or the conclusion. They also did not use the audience data to test whether the audience composition explains the platform differences (R2 point 2). The reply to R1's structural suggestion is only a promise for future studies, which is acceptable.
issues.response_claim: The authors say they rewrote the Discussion to highlight audience characteristics as a limitation and recommend future studies.
issues.observed_change: A sentence on generalisability and a recommendation were added. The abstract and conclusion keep the strong claims, such as 'most effective way'.

evidence.exact_quote: suggesting that using images of people in combination with short text captions is the most effective way to engage social media audiences
potentially limiting the generalizability of the findings (Berkowitz & donnerstein, 1982)

evidence_limits: Per-post CSV data and the analysis code on Zenodo were not provided here, so the model, effect sizes and the additional type 3 repost results could not be checked.
Only the revised text and figures were available; no track-changes file, so the 'rewritten Discussion' claim was checked by comparing the before and after text.
The R1 reviewer's structural suggestions and the R1 reply (no changes) are low-stakes and not judged substantive.
answer.process_consistency_auxiliary: The R1 reply declines changes and the R2 reply claims a rewritten Discussion; comparing the versions shows only limited modification, so the reported level of revision is higher than what is visible.
